doc.title: Cal Collins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 11, 1997

chapter: Careers, business and the music scene
title: When jazz was popular and its decline around 1960
summary: Jazz faded from the 1950s as rock and roll took over; early rock sidemen still swung and Connie Kay played R&B.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: In your career, was there a time, what span of years would you say jazz was most popular?

Probably from the time I was born to — it seems like it started petering out in the 50s, somewhere in the 50s, we had to scuffle around. Of course there was a lot of bars that you could play, you know, cocktail lounges and all that, you could play some pretty nice, easy, light jazz. But it started petering out, especially around 1960, with more takeover from rock & roll. Of course country’s always been there. Everybody loves country music it seems like. But it started getting pretty rough around the 60s. About 1960.

It’s kind of interesting when you listen to some of the early rock & roll records, I notice Chuck Berry especially, is that he was moving into a rock & roll thing but the guys behind him were still playing swing. And there was this kind of bumpy transition.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. A lot of those guys played the straight ahead rhythm & blues, which I still like, you know the organ trios and all that I think really swing and it really sounds good. And they were sort of into that. Connie Kaye as a matter of fact, when he was younger, he played with the R&B bands quite a bit.

Yeah, with the back beat, the heavy back beat and all that stuff and Honky Tonk and whatever, some of those people. But they did change it to this other stuff, whatever it is, you were saying Chuck Berry’s sidemen were changing the way they played. I don’t know, rock & roll, I just really can’t — I don’t hate it, I’m just anti it.
